messages.subject: Re: Using variograms to categorise individuals behaviour
messages.subject_clean: Using variograms to categorise individuals behaviour
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

For deer11759 I've segmented only spatially and I didn't remove the migration bit because it only lasts one day - but I can try to identify it and remove it. In general these deers are very quick in moving from an area to the next one. Do you think I should segment the data in time based on the variogram?
For deer9050, the variogram is zoomed out 90%. The others, it depends, normally if the zoom 50% gives me a clear interpretation of the data I leave it as it is, if I see some temporal pattern I zoom it out up to 90%. Should I consider only the 50% zoom? I normally ignore the end bits of variograms zoomed 90%.
In these particular  variograms:
deer9050: 90%
deer11759_all + area1 + area2: 50%
deer9044: 50%
deer9052: 50%
deer11289: 90%
deer11746: 50%
deer11760: 50%
deer11766: 50%
deer11762: 50%
deer11765: 50%
deer9049: 50%

Thanks for the overlap link (and for everything),

Best Regards,

Licia

On Fri, 29 Nov 2019, 02:34 Christen Fleming, <chris.h...@gmail.com> wrote:

> deer11759_area1 looks like it has some migration or other area in it. Did you remove the migration bit? Did you segment in time or just spatially?
>
> 9050_stationary kind of looks like a shifting range that came back. Are these variograms zoomed out 50% (default) or 100%?
>
> You can check overlap between years, yes. See the example here: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/overlap.html
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Thursday, November 28, 2019 at 12:13:15 PM UTC-5, Licia Calabrese wrote:
> > Dear Chris,
> >
> > Thank you very much for your reply.
> >
> > It could be that deer11759_area1_stationary looks crazy because it has some missing data, as it is complementary with deer11759_area2_stationary (I've isolated the two areas where I could see the deer was more or less stable), isn't it?
> > On the contrary, deer 9050_stationary doesn't have many missing data and l don't really know how to interpret it, could it be dispersal?
> > These deers don't really follow a summer/winter range segregation but I can try to isolate those periods and see what happens. I'm also trying to isolate the different ranges for the migratory individuals, taking also into account the different years. With the function overlap()can I check in HRs overlap between different years? To do do that I guess I have to calculate a ctmm HR per each period (winter/summer) each deer and each year, include them in a list and use the function overlap(). Am I right? Sorry but I've never used the function overlap()with ctmm package.
> >
> > Thanks again for your help!
> >
> > Best Regards,
> >
> > Licia
> >
> > On Wednesday, November 27, 2019 at 9:58:05 PM UTC+1, Christen Fleming wrote:
> > > Hi Licia,
> > >
> > > 9049_migratory, 11746_stationary, 11759_all, deer11759_area2_stationary, 11760_migratory all appear to have some amount of annual migration in them because for short time lags and for 12 month time lags the deer is much closer to where it started than for 6 month time lags. Many deer have a "migration" that is very short, like moving into your neighbor's house. deer11759_area2_stationary doesn't appear to be terribly segmented, but deer11759_area1_stationary looks crazy. Moreover, I don't understand how either is segmented with 12+ months of data. Naively, I would segment the tracks in to winter range, summer range, and migration components, which would give the summer and winter ranges large gaps of missing data during the winter and summer, respectively.
> > >
> > > 11289_ambiguous looks dispersal in that the variogram just continues to increase with time lag. 11766_stationary looks more ambiguous to me.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Chris
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, November 27, 2019 at 6:04:37 AM UTC-5, Licia Calabrese wrote:
> > > > Dear Christen,
> > > >
> > > > I'm working with GPS data of 11 deers and I'm trying to categorise each individual behaviour using the ctmm variograms. After that I will calculate the respective HRs.
> > > > Sometimes I have difficulties interpreting the variogram and to decide whether the individual behaviour is stationary, migrant or irregular (ambiguous).
> > > > I attach the variograms with the categorisation I gave them, could you please confirm/reject my guess?
> > > > In particular, I have many doubts for the deers 11765, 9050 and 11289.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks a lot!
> > > >
> > > > Licia
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > --
> > > > Licia Calabrese, PhD
> > > > Conservation Biologist

messages.subject: Re: Using variograms to categorise individuals behaviour
messages.subject_clean: Using variograms to categorise individuals behaviour
messages.body_plain:
Hi Licia,

For segmenting migrations, if it isn't easy to do visually, I would recommend either R package marcher or spatio-temporal clustering (can't remember the R package at the moment).
Segmenting with the variogram is hard, because the x-axis represents relative time lags and not absolute time, but using the variogram as a check for residence after segmenting is a good idea.
I don't have a general recommendation on the zoom level, but zooming out can be useful when the data and model don't appear to match, initially. Usually, in that case the variogram trends upward (possibly out of plotting range) due to a range shift of some kind.

Best,
Chris

I hope you don't mind me jumping in! I've been struggling with the same thing and have tried with macher and a few other methods. One package I've played around with recently that seems to work pretty well for many of my animals is segclust2d. In case it helps!

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/segclust2d/vignettes/segclust.html
https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1365-2656.13105

All the best,

Gen

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris and All,

I’m using the function overlap() to assess the overlap between winter and summer range in deers. It's the first time I'm using it and I have two questions/doubts:

1.     If the summer or winter range of the deer are not stationary I cannot use overlap(), as the HR estimate won’t be correct. Is it right? In such case, I have to use classic HR estimators such as KDE; however (if I understood correctly  from the paper “Statistical inference for home range overlap”) I cannot use the ctmm overlap method on HRs computed with estimators other than AKDE, is that correct? Is there anything else I can use from the ctmm environment? In the past I used to use the function kerneloverlap() from the adehabitatHR package but it doesn’t give a statistical significance.

2.   After calculating the overlap between two stationary HRs with the overlap(), how can I test if the overlap is significant or not? For example, an overlap of  0.9246951 (0.8880717- 0.954848) is probably significant, but is there a coefficient that can assess that? (i. e. the Bhattacharyya coefficient) and how can I extract it? And if it was overlap ≅ 0.55?

Thank you very much for your help,

Licia

messages.subject: Re: overlap() significance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Licia,

1. AKDE is more general than KDE. With the current models in ctmm, AKDE is for stationary or approximately stationary movement processes. KDE further requires that the data is not autocorrelated. If AKDE is not appropriate, then KDE is not appropriate either. KDE is accessible within ctmm when using an IID model in the akde().

2. You want to test if there is significant overlap? Test overlap>0? I am not sure if that would be a tractable test. For two Gaussian distributions, that would be testing whether the two means are infinitely far apart relative to their standard deviations. That doesn't seem well posed to me.

More straightforward is to test if overlap is greater than some threshold>0. overlap() reports two-sided 95% CIs with level=0.95 by default. You can trick this into two one-sided 95% CIs by setting level to 0.90, which then places 5% alpha on each side.

Best,
Chris

thanks!

messages.subject: doubt of use: weights=TRUE option
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christen,

I have a question with regard to the weights=TRUE option to adjust for irregular sampling. We have collected telemetry data in 10 minutes intervals during 3 week periods for 37 free-ranging dogs. We have filtered the data to sort out erronous fixes that might have been caused by dogs under houses by calculating GPS errors in a systematic way. We further programmed the GPS to only collect data when the dogs were moving.That said, we don't have fixed 10 minutes intervals (but not related to a systematic sampling error, but to dog behaviour), but we also have some dogs where data was not collected during a whole day or even several days, probably due to misfunction of the GPS. I have read through your publication "Correcting for missing and irregular data in home-range estimation" and I find that the examples given there are more extreme than our data with regard to irregularity. Still, I tried to use the weights=TRUE option, but I have not managed to run it yet, it takes hours.

Do you think it is ok to keep the option weights=FALSE in our case? Or what can be done to fasten up? I have also tried with fast=TRUE.
Thanks very much for your opinion,

cheers
Elke

messages.subject: Re: doubt of use: weights=TRUE option
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elke,

I am updating the documentation in help('bandwidth') to say the following:

The weights=TRUE argument can be used to correct temporal sampling bias caused by autocorrelation.weights=TRUE will optimize n=length(data$t) weights via constrained & preconditioned conjugate gradient algorithms. These algorithms have a few options that should be considered if the data are very irregular.

fast=TRUE grids the data with grid width dt and applies FFT algorithms, for a computational cost as low as O(n \log n)with only O(n) function evaluations. If no dt is specified, the minimum sampling interval min(diff(data$t)) is used. If the data are irregular (permitting gaps), then dt may need to be several times smaller to avoid slow down. In this case, try setting trace=TRUE and decreasing dt until the interations speed up and the number of feasibility assessments becomes less than O(n). On the other hand, if the data contain some very tiny time intervals, say 1 second among hourly sampled data, then the default dt setting will create an excessively high-resolution discretization of time, which will also cause slowdown. In this case CTMM should contain an error model and dt can likely be increased to a larger fraction of the median sampling interval.

fast=FALSE uses exact times and has a computational cost as low as O(n^2), including O(n^2) function evaluations. With PC="direct" this method will produce a result that is exact to within machine precision, but with a computational cost of O(n^3). fast=FALSE,PC='direct' is often the fastest method with small datasets, where n ≤ O(1,000), but scales terribly with larger datasets.

In your case, I would try the exact method if your datasets only contain ~400 locations.

Best,
Chris
